summary: A second outlet carrying the former master Andrew Donald, published a day after HGPTV's account and covering the same allegations at greater length: twelve years of chronic overloading, inadequate watertight subdivision, bilge systems he says could not control flooding, a single-hull design he considers unfit for passengers, and delayed dry-docking. It is corroboration of what HGPTV reported, not a second witness — both rest on Donald alone. It adds his account of why he spoke when he did, and his statement that management "have the power to load, overload and set sailing time" and then "back-pedalled and left the captain in all the mess". He names nobody, nothing in it is independently verified, and this archive adopts none of it.

The document that converts the wreck question from a consultation into a procurement. MARAD, under the Ministry of Public Utilities and Aviation, has invited expressions of interest from marine salvage contractors, with submissions due 14 August. Two things in it matter beyond the decision itself. The state describes the hull, in its own words, as carrying "forensic evidence for the ongoing Commission of Inquiry" — the first time in this corpus that it has said so. And the notice supplies physical particulars the record has lacked: the wreck's position, a depth of 13 to 15 metres, twin Caterpillar C18 engines, and a length of 38.6 metres, which does not agree with the 40.26 metres carried elsewhere here. MARAD reserves the right to cancel the process.

The second source on the salvage invitation, which takes it out of single-source territory, and which states the evidential purpose plainly: the recovered vessel is expected to assist the Commission of Inquiry in determining what caused the capsizing, and bidders must show how they will protect and document forensic evidence. What it does not carry — and what no state document in this corpus carries — is any explanation from the government of why it is now salvaging, or any acknowledgement of the memorial proposal this supersedes.

The first report to name the salvage procurement for what it also is: the abandonment of the memorial proposal that went to families on 25 July. The reversal was not announced — it was communicated through a procurement notice — and the reason given, mounting public and family pressure, is the newspaper's characterisation rather than the government's, because no state document in this corpus acknowledges a change of position at all. The piece recalls the Opposition Leader's earlier language about the memorial plan, including an allegation of attempted cover-up that this archive records as his and does not adopt.

The opposition's response to the salvage decision, and it moves the argument from whether to raise the vessel to how fast. APNU's Ganesh Mahipaul argues that an expression-of-interest process closing on 14 August pushes the start of salvage to late August or early September once evaluation, bidding, contracting and mobilisation are counted, and calls for emergency procurement instead: "That timeline is simply unacceptable." His sharpest point is that the evidence the notice exists to protect is decaying while the process runs — "Salt water is unforgiving." No government response appears. The report also carries figure errors — the sinking dated to 19 July, and the survivor and fatality counts inverted — which are recorded here as the outlet's, not as a movement in the record.
